text: SSDs wear out because of the way flash memory stores data. Each cell holds information as electrical charge trapped in a floating gate or charge-trap layer, and writing or erasing that charge means forcing electrons through a thin insulating oxide. Every program/erase cycle damages that insulator a little, until the cell can't hold charge reliably enough to tell its voltage levels apart. TLC (triple-level cell) flash stores three bits in each cell, so it needs precise voltages and typically survives only about 3,000 of these cycles. That sounds low, but drives are designed to make that budget last. Wear leveling is how the controller spreads writes across the blocks so no single area burns out early while others sit unused, even when the same file is rewritten over and over. Over-provisioning helps too: manufacturers often reserve about 7% of the raw capacity as spare space the user never sees. The controller uses it to move data around during garbage collection, cut down on extra writes, and swap in fresh blocks for worn ones. Together, these techniques let a typical SSD last for years of normal use.
